newsitem.title: USA: Weather threatens U.S. shuttle launch.
newsitem.headline: Weather threatens U.S. shuttle launch.

text.p: U.S. space agency managers, worried by the dismal weather forecast for Tuesday's planned launch of the space shuttle Columbia, will decide on Monday whether to postpone blast-off until later in the week, officials said.

U.S. Air Force meteorologists offered a grim forecast for the shuttle's planned 2:37 p.m. EDT (1837 GMT) blastoff from Florida's Kennedy Space Centre. They gave the shuttle only a 10 percent chance of fair weather for launch.
Thunderstorms and rain showers were expected to form along the east coast of Florida and there was also potential for severe weather that could damage an exposed shuttle on the launch pad.
NASA managers have the option to move the shuttle's two and a half hour launch window into the evening, but the storms are unlikely to abate.
"If we can get off the ground it's going to be early (afternoon)," shuttle weather officer Ed Priselac told a news conference on Monday.
Mission managers would review the weather at a 10:30 a.m. EDT (1430 GMT) meeting and decide whether to delay the launch to take advantage of a better weather forecast for later in the week.
Engineers reported no technical problems with Columbia, the oldest of NASA's four space shuttles.
The winged spaceship is to make a second attempt at a 16-day research mission that was cut short in April after just five days because of a troublesome power generator.
